newsitem.title: GABON: Gabon voters smash ballot boxes claiming fraud.
newsitem.headline: Gabon voters smash ballot boxes claiming fraud.

text.p: Gabon's first multi-party municiapal elections degenerated into chaos when people protesting at voting delays and claiming widespread fraud broke open ballot boxes and threw voting papers onto the streets.
Crowds of angry voters ran through streets in Libreville, the capital of the Central African state, that were littered with ballot papers which they said had been stuffed into boxes.
"We are in in a false Gabon, a rotten Gabon. It's not worth having elections in our country," said one voter shown on national television news.
Another voter, speaking outside a polling station which was still closed 12 hours after voting had been set to start, said: "The boxes have been stuffed in advance."

The president of the National Electoral Commission, Gilbert Ngoulakia, said the elections would be not be cancelled even though some polling stations failed to open and voting cards did not reach others.
"On the whole things have gone well," he said in a midnight television. "The rest of Gabon is not necessarily the same as Libreville," he added, refering to the protests in the cpaital.

The municipal elections were organised as part of a wider deal between the government and the opposition after violent social and political disturbances over the disputed election of President Omar Bongo to a five-year term in 1993.

Bongo, leader of the deeply-entrenched Parti Democratique Gabonais, has ruled the former French colony since 1968. He began moves towards a multi-party system in 1990 after a rash of strikes and demonstrations by workers and students.
Five people were killed in opposition unrest triggered by Bongo's 1993 victory and a further nine were killed in 1994 after the country's French-supported CFA franc was devalued.
Voting throughout Libreville and major towns was plagued on Sunday by non-delivery of voting cards, outdated electoral lists and an absence of officials.

Many voting centres remained closed with queues of voters watched by heavily-armed police and troops. Water cannon, armoured personnel carriers and troops carrying tear gas and grenade launchers were on standby throughout Libreville.
Officials said angry voters had blockaded election officials in their offices in the country's second city, Port Gentil, the hub of its oil industry.

"The election is completely chaotic. They (voters) started smashing the booths at the town of Fougamou when their papers and lists did not arrive," said Mengome Atome, vice-president of the elctoral commission.
Electoral officials said they had asked for the vote to be delayed until October 30 to allow preparations and voter registrations to be completed. "The request was refused," said one official.
He said there had not been enough time to register the names of 400,000 voters on the commission's computerised voting sytem, designed to avoid electoral fraud.

Gabon's 1.2 million people are concentrated in the main cities of Libreville, Franceville and Port Gentil. Many left Libreville to vote for independant candidates in rural areas, election officials said.
